title: Eigenvectors, SVD and PCA

objectives.text: Verify real symmetric eigenpairs and relate centered-data singular values to covariance eigenvalues without relying on eigenvector sign or arbitrary repeated-eigenspace bases.
Compute and interpret a training-centered PCA projection with explicit sample normalization, feature scaling and held-out transformation boundaries.

blocks.markdown: An eigenpair of a square matrix A is a scalar λ and NONZERO vector v with Av=λv. A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues. PSD matrices have nonnegative eigenvalues; PD matrices have strictly positive ones. Eigenvectors can be rescaled, so a direction is not automatically a unit vector. For variance/projection calculations using an orthonormal basis, normalize and check the basis rather than inserting an arbitrary multiple.

blocks.source:
matrix = [[3,1],[1,3]]
for value, vector in [(4,[1,1]), (2,[1,-1])]:
    product = [sum(a*x for a,x in zip(row,vector)) for row in matrix]
    print(product == [value*x for x in vector])
print(sum(x*x for x in [1,1]))
# A normalized eigenvector has norm1; [1,1] is an eigenvector but not unit length.
blocks.caption: Expected output: True, True, then 2. For [[3,1],[1,3]], directions (1,1) and (1,-1) have eigenvalues 4 and 2. Each listed direction has squared length 2, so divide by sqrt(2) for unit-vector projection/variance formulas. v=0 is excluded from an eigenpair because it would satisfy the equation for every λ.

blocks.markdown: If v is a unit eigenvector, -v describes the same axis. Its scores flip sign, but vvᵀ and reconstructed projections do not. With a repeated eigenvalue, any orthonormal basis within that eigenspace is valid; near-repeated eigenvalues can make individual directions sensitive. Compare eigenpair residuals, orthonormality and relevant subspace/projector behavior, not a hardcoded sign or exact component list. This lesson is about real symmetric covariance, not a claim that every real nonsymmetric matrix has real orthogonal eigenvectors.

Let training X have n≥2 observations as rows and d features as columns. Fit training column mean μ and set Z=X-μ. Choose sample covariance C=ZᵀZ/(n-1). For unit direction v, variance of centered scores Zv is vᵀCv. Choosing the largest-eigenvalue direction maximizes that variance; choosing the top k orthonormal directions gives PCA's Euclidean least-squares reconstruction subspace. This criterion preserves training variance, not necessarily predictive, causal or economically useful information. To see the maximum, write unit v in an orthonormal eigenbasis as v=sum_i alpha_i*q_i, with sum_i alpha_i²=1. Then vᵀCv=sum_i lambda_i*alpha_i²≤lambda_max. Equality holds in a largest-eigenvalue eigenspace. For retained orthonormal columns V_k, scores T=Z V_k and reconstructed rows are T V_kᵀ+μ. Each row uses its nearest point in this fitted affine subspace; squared training reconstruction error equals the sum of discarded s_i². Keeping the largest s_i minimizes that discarded sum among rank-k orthogonal subspaces.

A thin singular-value decomposition writes Z=U S Vᵀ with nonnegative singular values s_i on diagonal S, sorted from largest to smallest. U and V have orthonormal columns in their thin factors. Then ZᵀZ=V S²Vᵀ, so nonzero covariance eigenvalues are λ_i=s_i²/(n-1), NOT s_i/(n-1). Directions are columns of V; a library returning Vᵀ stores them in rows. With d>n the thin factors do not list a complete zero-eigenvalue nullspace, though they can represent the nonzero principal directions.

blocks.title: Track the denominator and the coordinate orientation

steps.text: ZᵀZ=diag(8,2). Under n-1=3 sample normalization, covariance eigenvalues are 8/3 and 2/3. Their sum 10/3 is total sample variance.

The singular values are sqrt(8),sqrt(2). Squaring and dividing by 3 gives the same covariance eigenvalues. Dividing by n=4 instead would give 2 and 1/2, changing variances but not these axes or explained-variance ratios.

The first component explains (8/3)/(10/3)=0.8 of the training variance. Its unit direction is the first coordinate axis up to sign; a later row (14,20) projects/reconstructs exactly using the TRAINING mean and axis.

blocks.markdown: The next illustration requires NumPy in a separately prepared environment. It remains a readable worked example when the app has no verified NumPy capability; answering the lesson does not require installing anything. App execution is disabled for this block until the actual dependency/runtime is qualified. Record the Python and NumPy versions used for local reproduction.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
# Rows are training observations; columns are two compatible-scale features.
train = np.array([[12.,20.],[8.,20.],[10.,21.],[10.,19.]])
mean = train.mean(axis=0)
centered = train - mean
covariance = centered.T @ centered / (len(train)-1)
values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(covariance)  # ascending; vectors are columns
order = np.argsort(values)[::-1]
values, basis = values[order], vectors[:,order]
u, singular, vh = np.linalg.svd(centered, full_matrices=False)
scores = centered @ basis
print(mean.tolist())
print(np.round(values,6).tolist())
print(np.round(singular**2/(len(train)-1),6).tolist())
print(np.round(np.var(scores,axis=0,ddof=1),6).tolist())
print(np.round(values/values.sum(),6).tolist())
print(np.allclose(covariance @ basis, basis*values, rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12))
# Compare rank-one projectors, not arbitrary eigenvector signs.
print(np.allclose(basis[:,:1] @ basis[:,:1].T, vh[:1].T @ vh[:1], rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12))
# Later data use the TRAINING mean and basis, without refitting.
later = np.array([[14.,20.]])
reconstructed = ((later-mean) @ basis[:,:1]) @ basis[:,:1].T + mean
print(np.round(reconstructed,6).tolist())
blocks.caption: Expected output: [10.0, 20.0]; [2.666667, 0.666667] on each of the next three lines; [0.8, 0.2]; True; True; then [[14.0, 20.0]]. The checks are small-fixture floating tolerances 1e-12, not universal. eigh returns ascending eigenvalues/column eigenvectors while SVD returns descending singular values/rows of Vh. The example sorts both PCA eigenvalues and their associated columns together and compares sign-invariant rank-one projectors.

blocks.markdown: PCA centers but does not automatically standardize features. Measuring one feature in cents instead of dollars can change covariance PCA axes and variance ratios; choose common scales or a stated training-only standardization. Standardization itself changes the geometry and needs a zero-variance-column policy. If total training variance is 0, explained-variance ratios are undefined and should not be reported as a meaningful set of percentages. A zero/near-zero eigenvalue also matters before whitening or dividing by a component standard deviation; whitening is not implemented here.

Constructing ZᵀZ explicitly squares the 2-norm condition number when Z has full column rank. Direct SVD can avoid forming that Gram matrix and is often preferable for difficult data. This is not a claim that every implementation/problem is stable or that numerical tiny negative eigenvalues should be clipped without a scale-aware policy. The covariance and SVD paths are compared here only on a small well-separated fixture. Repeated-eigenvalue directions must be evaluated as subspaces.

Fit μ, any scaling and the component basis on training rows only. Transform later rows with those frozen quantities; refitting on the full dataset leaks the evaluation distribution. Choice of component count and other preprocessing belongs in development/validation, not repeated inspection of a final test set. High explained training variance does not establish out-of-sample predictive usefulness or a causal factor model; low-variance directions can still carry a target-specific signal.

Independent transfer: verify Av=λv for the two exact directions and normalize them. Derive λ=s²/(n-1) from the thin SVD rather than memorizing a library attribute. Change the covariance denominator from n-1 to n and identify which values change. Then add an offset to all training rows and show centered covariance stays fixed. Propose tests for constant columns, all-constant data, a repeated eigenvalue and held-out centering without requiring one arbitrary eigenvector sign.

References: [NumPy symmetric eigenpairs](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.eigh.html), [SVD factors/orientation](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.svd.html), [Princeton PCA/SVD derivation](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring19/cos324/files/pca.pdf), and [PCA centering/sample-variance convention](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.decomposition.PCA.html). Own text derives the SQUARED singular-value scaling explicitly and uses n-1 consistently. No scikit-learn execution or professional factor-model qualification is claimed.

summary: PCA needs training centering, a declared covariance denominator/feature geometry and sign/subspace-aware eigen checks. Covariance eigenvalues are squared singular values divided by the chosen denominator; explained variance is not a prediction guarantee.
